title: The little ones
hookLine: Jesus warns fiercely against harming children (Matthew 18:6)

cards: The disciples are arguing about rank. They ask Jesus straight out: who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? Matthew says Jesus calls a little child over and sets the child in the middle of them.
Just a small person standing in a circle of grown men who were, a minute ago, comparing themselves. Unless they become like this child, Jesus says, they won't enter the kingdom at all.
Then comes a warning with no softness in it.

teach.b: "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea."
A millstone was the heavy stone for grinding grain. Better, Jesus says, to sink than to do this.
Offend, there, doesn't mean hurt someone's feelings. The Greek is about making someone stumble, setting a trap in their path. To cause a child to fall, in body or in faith, is what he warns against.
A few verses later: "Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven."
Children, in this picture, aren't small and forgettable. They have someone watching in the highest court there is.
In Mark's Gospel, when the disciples try to shoo parents and children away, Jesus is indignant: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not." Suffer there means allow.

These words have a hard edge for churches today. Day one hundred forty-three named church hurt; here it reaches the youngest. Churches have had to face abuse within their own walls, and the failure to protect children.
Some now answer with practical things: background checks, two adults in every room, clear ways to report, and listening to survivors.
If a child is in danger, call local emergency help; if this stirs up something of your own, in the US you can call or text 988. Jesus didn't put the child at the edge of the circle.
He put the child in the middle.

how: Churches teach Jesus's care for children in Sunday school and preaching, and some congregations now train volunteers in child safeguarding, require background checks, and keep two adults with children at all times.

games.q: you're Jesus. your disciples want to know which of them is the greatest in the kingdom. what do you do?
o: call a little child and set him in the middle of them.
tell them it's not their business.
games.why: he calls a child into the middle of the circle and tells them to become like this child. then he warns, fiercely, against harming one.

practice: Bring to mind one child you're connected to, your own or someone else's, and picture them in the middle of the circle.

Then ask a plain question: what would make them a little safer, a seat belt checked, an adult who listens, knowing who to call if something seems wrong? If you pray, you can pray for that child by name.

wordCard.voice: The little ones. Jesus's name for children, and for the small and trusting, set in the middle and fiercely protected in Matthew 18.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 18:6: causes to stumble; the King James Bible says offend.

carryVoice: Your line: protect the little ones. In Matthew, their angels see the Father's face. Same time tomorrow.
